G2i explains AI labs’ data purchasing decisions at AI Engineer CODE 2026

At AI Engineer CODE 2026, G2i founder Gabe Greenberg discussed how frontier AI labs decide whether to pay more for exclusive training data or take a discount on data another lab can also buy, and when it makes sense to build a data operation in‑house.

🔍 Overview

  • Labs can pay more for training data they keep exclusive, or take a discount on data that other labs can also buy.
  • Small pilot orders often turn into larger engagements.
  • Decision factors were explained by Gabe Greenberg during the event recorded in San Francisco.

🧩 How labs choose data

  • Evaluate the cost of exclusivity versus shared‑discount models.
  • Start with pilot orders to test value before scaling up.
  • Consider building an internal data operation when long‑term needs justify it.

⚙️ Task design process

  • A good training task should sit just ahead of what a model can do today.
  • Senior engineers design the task, choose the starting data, and build a verifier that can score the result.
  • Gabe explained these steps as part of G2i’s workflow.

🤝 G2i’s role

item.title: Misata Introduces Declarative Synthetic Data Generation with Verification
item.description:
Misata Introduces Declarative Synthetic Data Generation with Verification

Misata is a new declarative synthetic data generator for Python. It allows developers to write down the facts a dataset must satisfy, and the engine builds multi-table data that satisfies all of them simultaneously.

🧩 How it works

Users define invariants in a misata.yaml file, such as monthly revenue curves, balanced ledgers, or foreign key constraints. The system generates rows derived from these specifications.

  • Specification as Ground Truth: The specification is the ground truth, and the rows are derived from it. For example, if the specification states “January revenue is 180,000,” this is true before a single row exists.
  • DuckDB Integration: Once data is generated, DuckDB checks the files on disk and writes a certificate that anyone can re-run.
  • Independent Verification: The verify.py script uses only the standard library and duckdb. It shares no code with the generator.

⚙️ Key details

The tool addresses the “oracle problem” in testing, where verifying data pipelines requires both input data and an independently known answer. Traditional methods have limitations:

  • Copying Production: Provides data without a known answer.
  • Hand-written Fixtures: Provide an answer that rots.
  • Random Generators: Provide data whose answer must be computed by the code under test.

In a documented example, Misata generated data satisfying 69 invariants, including:

  • Twelve monthly revenue totals (e.g., 180,000.00 in January, 240,000.00 in June).
  • Channel splits inside each month.
  • Planned row counts per month.
  • Zero orphaned customer_ids and unique keys.

The verification process can detect specific failures, such as a mismatched SHA256 hash or a precision error where an observed value of 180000.01 does not match the expected 180000.00.

🚀 Availability

Misata is available for Python. It can be installed and used as follows:

# Installation
pip install "misata[duckdb]"

# Data Generation

# Verification

A successful verification outputs a certificate indicating that files match their attested SHA256 hashes and all invariants hold.

item.title: Mostly AI engine enables flexible tabular and text model reuse
item.description:
Mostly AI engine enables flexible tabular and text model reuse

🔍 Overview

A new library, mostlyai-engine, serves as the core model engine for the Mostly AI Synthetic Data SDK. It allows users to train models on flat or sequential data and flexibly reuse them for various downstream tasks without retraining. The engine supports two primary model classes: TabularARGN for structured tabular data and LanguageModel for semi-structured textual tabular data.

🧩 How it works

The TabularARGN class provides a scikit-learn-compatible interface for working with structured, flat, or sequential tabular data. Once trained, models can be reused for regression, classification, imputation, and sampling. Key training and generation capabilities include:

  • Control training time and parameters
  • Monitor training progress
  • Optionally enable differential privacy
  • Optionally provide context data
  • Up-sample or down-sample
  • Conditionally generate
  • Rebalance categories
  • Impute missing values
  • Incorporate fairness

⚙️ Key details

The library supports synthetic data generation, classification, regression, and imputation through a few lines of Python code. Users can load data, train the model, and perform tasks such as:

  • Generating new synthetic samples
  • Generating new synthetic samples conditionally
  • Filling in missing values
  • Predicting categorical or numerical target columns
  • Assessing marginal conditional probability for one or more target columns

A companion tool, mostlyai-qa, is used to assess the fidelity and novelty of synthetic samples with respect to original samples. It calculates accuracy, similarity, and distance metrics, visualizes statistics for comparison against training and holdout samples, and generates a standalone HTML summary report. It supports analyzing single-table data, sequential data, and sequential data with context.

🚀 Availability

The latest release of mostlyai-engine can be installed via uv. It is highly recommended to install the package within a dedicated virtual environment. For GPU setups required for LLM finetuning and inference, specific installation instructions are provided. On Linux, users can explicitly install the CPU-only variant of PyTorch together with mostlyai-engine. The mostlyai-qa package is available via pip install -U mostlyai-qa.

item.title: NVIDIA Megatron Core Supports Market Forecasting via Patch Embeddings
item.description:
NVIDIA Megatron Core Supports Market Forecasting via Patch Embeddings

NVIDIA has released a workflow for applying Megatron Core, its open-source library for training transformer models at scale, to financial market forecasting. The approach processes stream data—trades and quotes timestamped to the microsecond—into model-ready tensors to predict returns and trading volume.

🔍 Overview

The core task involves aggregating high-frequency market data into bars, where each row represents one instrument per time unit with price, volume, and other statistics. A preprocessing script converts these intraday market bars into tensors for the Megatron distributed training loop. Unlike methods that tokenize market values into text, this pipeline uses learned patch embeddings to turn groups of observations into model inputs.

🧩 How it works

The preprocessing pipeline groups consecutive bars for a single instrument on a specific trading day into patches, which serve as the model’s tokens. Fixed-length context windows are then slid over these patches.

  • Patching: Eight bars per patch and 32 patches per window create a sequence of 32 model positions containing 256 observations.
  • Inputs: The model receives patches with shape (B, L, P, F), instrument IDs (inst_id), and patch times of day (patch_tod).
  • Targets: Each window includes future targets for every context position, allowing one forward pass to produce forecasts throughout the context rather than just at the end.
  • Loss Function: The loss expects a dictionary containing return and volume share tensors of shape (B, L, H), representing one forecast per context position and horizon.

⚙️ Key details

  • Data Format: Input is a directory of Parquet files with columns for Symbol, Date, Timestamp, Close, and Volume, plus optional numeric feature columns.
  • Feature Engineering: The script derives within-day log returns and log volumes, ensuring the overnight gap never enters the inputs. Price and volume remain continuous features.
  • Instrument Specificity: Each training window includes the instrument identifier, allowing the model to learn instrument-specific behavior within shared parameters.
  • Metadata: Preprocessing records patch size, context length, and forecast horizons in saved metadata, making data configuration an explicit part of each experiment.

💡 Why it matters

This implementation demonstrates that standard transformer training infrastructure can be adapted for continuous financial time series by treating bars as patches rather than discrete tokens. The flexibility of the forward_step interface allows any MegatronModule taking the specified inputs and returning the target dictionary to be used in the training loop.

#Megatron #Transformer #TimeSeries #FinancialAI #NVIDIA

Source: Prepare Market Data for Forecasting with NVIDIA Megatron Core | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Databricks Launches Native Lakebase Sink for Apache Spark Structured Streaming
item.description:
Databricks Launches Native Lakebase Sink for Apache Spark Structured Streaming

Databricks has announced the general availability of a native Lakebase sink for Apache Spark™ Structured Streaming, simplifying real-time data ingestion into its serverless PostgreSQL offering. The connector eliminates the need for custom foreach writers, reducing complexity in building low-latency feature pipelines for use cases like fraud detection and recommendation systems.

📣 What Happened

Today, Databricks is releasing the native Lakebase sink for Apache Spark™ Structured Streaming. This connector writes computed results directly to Lakebase and handles batching, retries, and upserts automatically, removing the burden of building and maintaining custom infrastructure.

🔍 Why It Matters

Low-latency use cases such as fraud detection, live personalization, and real-time feature computation require results in a serving-ready OLTP store. Lakebase Postgres is a fully managed, serverless PostgreSQL database with autoscaling, branching, native Unity Catalog integration, and sub-10ms reads. Previously, writing to Lakebase from a streaming pipeline required developers to build custom foreach writers to manage batching, retries, and upserts — a complex task that was difficult to scale and maintain.

The new native sink handles these concerns internally. You can wire up a Lakebase write in minutes with a single writeStream call, without needing to manage performance, tuning, or maintenance.

⚙️ Key Features

  • Fully managed, serverless PostgreSQL database with autoscaling and native Unity Catalog integration
  • Sub-10ms read latency
  • Native Lakebase sink for Apache Spark™ Structured Streaming
  • Supports both micro-batch and Real-Time Mode
  • Automatic upsert handling with upsertKey — maintains one row per key
  • Built-in connection pooling, batching, and retries
  • Seamless credentials management via running user or service principal
  • Table creation if it does not exist
  • Real-time data ingestion using .toTable() for Unity Catalog-registered tables
  • Direct write using format("postgresql") for non-Unity Catalog tables or external PostgreSQL databases

🧩 Use Case Example: Real-Time Recommendation Features

A video streaming platform wants to recommend videos by leveraging users’ recent activity. The pipeline ingests WATCH and LIKE events from Kafka, computes the last 6 videos watched and the last 3 liked per user, and upserts one feature row per user into Lakebase in hundreds of milliseconds. At inference time, a recommendation model looks up each user’s feature row by user_id to rank what to show next.

The pipeline uses transformWithState to maintain per-user state and emit one feature row per user, with writing to Lakebase handled by a single writeStream and .toTable() call.

🚀 Availability and Benchmarks

The native sink is now generally available. In testing, the pipeline processed ~20K events per second against 5 million active users using a 40-core classic compute (DBR 18 LTS) writing to an 8-CU Lakebase project with 5-minute RTM checkpoint intervals. End-to-end latency from Kafka input timestamp to row landing in Lakebase was 100–200 milliseconds, with query latency in single digits via Lakebase.

💬 Customer Feedback

  • “We stream real-time data into Lakebase so our risk agent can pull a user’s recent activity when it investigates an alert. We initially built that path with a custom ForeachWriter, which meant building and maintaining the write infrastructure ourselves. As part of our development work, we found that the native sink reduces the custom work required for connection pooling, batching, and retries.” — Maria Marinova, Sr. Lead Software Engineer, DraftKings
  • “Testing real-time data flows into Lakebase is an important part of validating how our risk agent can quickly access the freshest available user data when making decisions. As we evaluated the native sink, we found that its built-in connection pooling, batching, and retries reduce the custom infrastructure we need to build and maintain.” — Georgi Stoychev, Sr. Software Automation Engineer, DraftKings

📊 Technical Details

Feature Description
Upsert Key Sink maintains one row per key
Connection Pooling Built-in, managed automatically
Batching Automatically handled for throughput
Retries Transient failure handling with backoff
Credentials Managed as running user or service principal
Table Creation Automatically created if not present
Latency End-to-end 100–200ms; query latency single-digit milliseconds

🔗 Getting Started

For a deeper look at the implementation, see the companion repo — a self-serve example you can run end-to-end.

item.title: Qdrant .NET Client Adds gRPC Support and TLS Configuration
item.description:
Qdrant .NET Client Adds gRPC Support and TLS Configuration

A new .NET client library for Qdrant has been released, allowing .NET applications to connect to the vector database at http://localhost:6334 using gRPC.

🔍 Overview

  • Install the library with dotnet add package Qdrant.Client.
  • The client connects by default to Qdrant on http://localhost:6334.
  • Internally, the high‑level client relies on a low‑level gRPC client to communicate with Qdrant.

🧩 How it works

  • The client creates a channel via QdrantChannel.ForAddress, which is used by both QdrantClient("localhost") and the ClientConfiguration overloads.
  • When the channel is created, the client automatically adds a qdrant-dotnet/<version> token to the request User-Agent alongside the gRPC library token.
  • This token enables server‑side tooling to attribute traffic to the .NET client and its version.
  • On .NET Framework, where the underlying channel handler must be configured manually, the token is not added automatically.

⚙️ Configuration options

  • Additional constructor overloads give developers more control over gRPC client configuration.
  • TLS can be configured, validating the server certificate using its thumbprint, and API‑key authentication can be added.
  • .NET Framework has limited support for gRPC over HTTP/2, but support can be enabled by:
    • Referencing System.Net.Http.WinHttpHandler version 6.0.1 or later.
    • Configuring WinHttpHandler as the inner handler for GrpcChannelOptions.

🚀 Usage example

await client.CreateCollectionAsync("my_collection", new VectorParams { Size = 100, Distance = Distance.Cosine });
// Query examples (illustrative):

📡 Compatibility notes

  • On .NET Framework, manual configuration of the channel handler is required, and the automatic User-Agent token is not added.
  • The client works out‑of‑the‑box on platforms where gRPC over HTTP/2 is supported without additional handlers.

item.title: New tool converts moderation policies into traceable preference data
item.description:
New tool converts moderation policies into traceable preference data

A new development called Preference Lab has been released, providing a workflow to turn content moderation policies into traceable preference data for machine learning and data teams. The tool allows users to define rules, generate boundary cases, and export candidate preference pairs that include original text, rule evidence, and decision history.

🧩 How It Works

The system operates by converting declarative policies into executable sequences. A PolicyPack declares language, labels, evidence requirements, scores, exceptions, and an ordered decision table using a fixed declarative vocabulary that cannot execute code. Every stage of the process uses the same compiled PolicyPack to ensure consistency.

Several components make up the release:

Component Status & Function
B Alpha Released; provides the synthesis kernel and run dashboard.
C Workbench Integrated into main but not yet released; adds human decisions and curated dataset versions.
PolicyPack Declarative file defining labels, evidence, and decision logic.

For teams building datasets, the tool checks structure, evidence references, and policy consistency via a passed gate. However, this gate does not turn machine decisions into human ground truth. The recorded workflow example provided with the release makes no external model calls and requires no API key.

⚙️ Technical Details

The tool is designed for Python 3.11 or 3.12 on macOS and Linux. The recorded demo operates locally and does not connect to external services.

  • Demo Output: Running the demo on five fixtures produces 1 completed case, 1 preference pair, and 4 abstentions.
  • Error Handling: The demo status is partial_failed with exit code 3 because four cases require external material not supplied by the demo. Diagnostics are saved rather than generating definitive answers for these cases.
  • Storage: Runs are stored under data/demo/runs/ and exports under data/datasets/demo/. Users can inspect pairs.jsonl for accepted pairs and manifest.json for policy and file hashes.
  • Data Preservation: Exports preserve original content, evidence, and policy identity to allow later inspection. SQLite checkpoints retain complete responses and stage results.

For live runs that send prompts to configured model providers, the tool enforces a budget cap and model price snapshot. Retries, usage estimates, and unsettled reservations remain visible. Unknown remote requests pause for an explicit decision instead of automatically repeating potentially charged calls.

🧪 Compatibility Checks

The system performs compatibility checks using actual loaders, templates, tokenization, and collators in separate pinned environments for:

  • TRL standard and conversational formats.
  • LLaMA-Factory ShareGPT.

Users can begin with the built-in Chinese handbook or the English contact-policy example.

🚀 Availability and Limitations

The project is not currently published to PyPI. For packaged installation, users should use the wheel and checksums available in the GitHub Releases. The affected 0.3.0a1 release has been withdrawn; users must use the corrected source or a later release.

The language and label schemas are open, but model quality across languages and specific training gains have not yet been established. Resuming a run requires the original rule, model, prompt, and code identities.

item.title: DeepFabric generates synthetic data for language model training
item.description:
DeepFabric generates synthetic data for language model training

DeepFabric is a tool designed to generate synthetic training data for language models and agent evaluations. It combines reasoning traces with tool-calling patterns to create high-quality, domain-specific datasets that teach models to think, plan, and act effectively, call tools correctly, and conform to strict schema structures.

🔍 Overview

The system distinguishes itself through unique topic graph generation algorithms that ensure high diversity while maintaining domain-anchored relevance. This approach guides sample creation to cover all necessary subtopics while avoiding redundancy, a common issue in other tools that can lead to model overfitting.

🧩 How it works

  • Data Generation: The process involves constrained decoding and response validation.
  • Tool Execution: Real tool executions occur within isolated webassembly environments.
  • Accuracy: These mechanisms ensure generated samples strictly adhere to structured schemas, variable constraints, and execution correctness, providing exact syntax and structure for training pipelines.
  • Tool Definitions: Tool definitions can be imported directly from MCP (Model Context Protocol) server schemas, automatically mocked, or based on real-life interfaces.
  • Standard Tools: A standard set of common tools, such as list_files() and read_file(), is included.

⚙️ Key details

  • Deployment Options: DeepFabric can be used as a library, a CLI tool, or via YAML configuration.
  • Configuration: The YAML configuration includes three main sections and optional shared LLM defaults.
  • Mocked Execution: Using mocked tool execution requires a running Spin service, which is provided in a Docker image.
  • Example Output: A specific configuration generated a topic graph with 27 unique nodes, resulting in 27 training samples saved to dataset.jsonl and achieving 100% topic coverage.

🚀 Availability

  • Integration: Generated datasets can be automatically uploaded to Hugging Face.
  • Training Frameworks: Data can be directly imported into popular training frameworks, including TRL, Unsloth, and Axolotl.
  • Evaluation: A built-in evaluation engine assesses model performance on unseen tasks derived from training splits, covering evaluation-only questions, answers, and tool traces.

item.title: Databricks introduces Genie ZeroOps for autonomous data pipeline issue resolution
item.description:
Databricks introduces Genie ZeroOps for autonomous data pipeline issue resolution

Databricks has introduced Genie ZeroOps, an autonomous agent that detects, investigates, and resolves data pipeline issues. Now available in Public Beta, ZeroOps automates the manual workflow of identifying and fixing pipeline issues, maintaining security, governance, and recommendation quality.

🔍 Overview

  • Genie ZeroOps is an autonomous agent that detects, investigates, and resolves data pipeline issues.
  • It automates the entire manual workflow from initial issue alert to a pull request.
  • ZeroOps maintains security, governance, and recommendation quality.

🧩 How it works

  • ZeroOps automatically triggers as soon as an issue is detected, without a prompt.
  • It reads run logs, source code, upstream table metadata, and samples, while respecting Unity Catalog permissions.
  • It uses Data Quality Monitoring to flag tables with issues related to freshness and completeness.
  • ZeroOps proposes fixes and can push them to a new branch for a pull request, never changing production code or data without direct approval.

⚙️ Key details

  • ZeroOps leverages direct access to Unity Catalog, metadata, and pipeline lineage.
  • It uses models hosted by Databricks inside their security perimeter, with model calls staying in the workspace’s region.
  • The model provider does not retain prompts or responses.
  • ZeroOps can be enabled by a workspace admin from the workspace Previews page.

🚀 Availability

  • Genie ZeroOps is available in Public Beta.
  • Workspace admins can turn it on from the workspace Previews page.
  • The ZeroOps banner can be found on the top of the pipelines page.

💡 Why it matters

  • Data engineering teams are overwhelmed, managing many thousands of pipelines a day.
  • Over half of pipeline issues require organization-specific knowledge to properly triage, rank, and resolve.
  • ZeroOps handles these complexities natively, leveraging direct access to your Unity Catalog, metadata, and pipeline lineage.
  • ZeroOps observed over 80,000 real customer issues across hundreds of companies during the private preview.
  • The new features added to help data teams triage issues faster include inbox sharing, notifications, one-click PR creation, and the ability to add custom business instructions.

📚 Documentation

  • Read the documentation here for more details on how to get started.
  • If your team needs help onboarding ZeroOps to production, reach out to your account team to inquire about any workshops that we offer.

item.title: Databricks Launches Interactive Reference Architecture for 70 Industries
item.description:
Databricks Launches Interactive Reference Architecture for 70 Industries

Databricks has released a public, interactive reference architecture board covering 70 industries across 11 economic sectors, designed to replace static, industry-specific slides that often drift out of date.

🏗️ The Problem with Static Diagrams

Previously, Databricks architecture discussions relied on standard slides showing ingestion, the lakehouse, and BI/AI. These generic visuals failed to specify how industry-specific systems—such as a bank’s SWIFT payment messages, a hospital’s HL7 and DICOM data, or a utility’s SCADA feeds—fit into the architecture. Industry-specific copies of these slides often became outdated with every product release and were stored locally, making it difficult to identify which versions were current.

🧩 How It Works

The new Databricks Reference Architecture is a public board updated directly from Databricks documentation to prevent staleness. Key features include:

  • Industry-Specific Boards: 70 distinct boards covering 11 economic sectors, with an industry picker for search and navigation.
  • Source Systems: 964 different source systems grouped by sector terminology (e.g., EHR and imaging in healthcare; metering and SCADA in utilities).
  • Data Formats: 186 industry-specific formats listed, including FIX and ISO 20022 for finance, HL7/FHIR for healthcare, and OPC UA for manufacturing.
  • Personas: 1,538 team personas (e.g., Treasury, ALM, Grid Operations) included across the boards.
  • Use Cases: 700 total use cases (10 per board) detailing the problem solved, the benefiting team, and the Databricks products used. 581 of these link to customer stories.

⚙️ Key Details

The architecture maintains a consistent Databricks Platform core while adapting the surrounding elements to each industry.

  • Medallion Layers: Use industry-specific terms for Bronze, Silver, and Gold layers. For example, the banking Gold layer holds net interest margin, while the healthcare Gold layer holds patient outcomes.
  • Views: Boards open in “Simplified” view, showing key systems and use cases. “Detailed” view adds CI/CD, monitoring, and operational stores.
  • Interactivity: Clicking any box opens a panel describing the item, its users, and learning resources. Users can toggle from generic types (e.g., EHR) to branded vendor products.
  • Learning Paths: Clicking a team persona generates a personalized learning path from Databricks Academy courses, certifications, and relevant demos.

💡 Why It Matters

This resource allows users to copy and modify boards to fit their own systems. It connects abstract architecture concepts to deployable assets, such as linking the Silver layer on the banking board to specific tables in the Databricks Industry Data Models. When a Databricks Solution Accelerator is available for a use case, the panel provides a direct link to working code.

#Databricks #DataArchitecture #AIInfrastructure #IndustryData #Lakehouse

item.title: Databricks introduces bulk migration for converting BI reports to AI/BI Dashboards
item.description:
Databricks introduces bulk migration for converting BI reports to AI/BI Dashboards

Databricks has made a new feature generally available that allows organizations to migrate multiple Business Intelligence (BI) reports to AI/BI Dashboards in a single run. This capability addresses the limitations of the previous one-report-at-a-time flow, which was suitable for pilots but resulted in a months-long manual grind for organizations with hundreds of reports. The bulk migration agent can now process an entire folder of reports from a single command.

🔍 Overview

The migration agent reads source BI files, generates corresponding AI/BI Dashboards on Databricks, and maps them to a specified target catalog and schema. Instead of importing reports individually, users can process many reports together. This extends the existing Databricks AI/BI migration experience to support batch processing from a single command.

🧩 How it works

To use this feature, users must ensure that partner-powered AI features are enabled at both the account and workspace levels. The migration process involves preparing source files and triggering the bulk flow through specific commands or natural language prompts.

File Preparation:

  • Export Tableau or Power BI reports to supported file types: .twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx, .pbit, or .tmdl.
  • For Tableau workbooks connecting to published data sources, export the data source (.tds or .tdsx) and place it next to the workbook.
  • Place all BI report files into a directory within a Unity Catalog volume. Note that bulk runs only pick up files from volumes; dragging files directly into the chat is only for single-report imports.

Triggering the Migration:

  • Directory-based: Pointing the command at a directory triggers the bulk flow for all reports in that folder.
  • Natural Language: Users can request, “Migrate every Power BI report in /Volumes/finance/bi/reports to AI/BI Dashboards.”
  • Specific Files: Users can name specific files, e.g., “Migrate Tableau reports Dashboard1.twb, Dashboard2.twb in /Volumes/finance/bi/reports to AI/BI Dashboards.”

⚙️ Key details

item.title: Databricks launches Genie Migrate for Serverless to automate classic-to-serverless migration
item.description:
Databricks launches Genie Migrate for Serverless to automate classic-to-serverless migration

Databricks has launched Genie Migrate for Serverless in beta, an agent that automates the migration of jobs and notebooks from classic compute to serverless compute. The agent handles configuration translation and presents changes as reviewable diffs, reducing migration from a manual research project to a review-and-approve step.

🔍 Overview

  • Serverless compute in Databricks removes the operational burden of managing infrastructure, automatically handling provisioning, scaling, and optimization.
  • Serverless usage has grown multifold in the past year, with thousands of customers running notebooks and jobs on it.
  • Most teams still have classic fleets they want to migrate to gain cost and operational benefits.
  • Manual migration has been difficult: flipping a job to serverless often produces errors, access-mode incompatibilities, Spark config issues, or missing libraries.

🧩 How it works

  • The agent runs from the /compute migrate slash command inside Genie on any job or notebook.
  • It is fully managed and requires no setup to start scanning.
  • Because Databricks manages it, the agent reads your job config and workload code inside your own workspace.
  • Before any changes, the agent scans your Jobs and Notebooks and marks each workload with its serverless readiness.
  • Once you pick an eligible workload, the agent proposes the changes needed for serverless and presents them for review before anything is written.
  • Nothing is applied until you approve it.
  • Every change, including code rewrites, is presented as a reviewable diff with a side-by-side comparison.
  • If the agent is unsure about something (for example, whether a Spark conf is still needed), it reports the conf rather than removing it.
  • For a larger fleet, you can run Genie Migrate for Serverless in the background with the Databricks CLI.
  • Your original job does not change until you review and approve its migration, and approving keeps the job’s ID, schedule, and permissions.

item.title: SageMaker HyperPod Inference Adds NVIDIA Dynamo Support for Distributed AI
item.description:
SageMaker HyperPod Inference Adds NVIDIA Dynamo Support for Distributed AI

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo, combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address challenges such as GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights exceeding the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead.

🧩 How it works

Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery.

The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components:

  • HyperPod Inference Operator: Manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource, using its dynamoSpec section to supply the Dynamo configuration.
  • Dynamo Operator: Manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD), including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements.
  • Grove: Coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships.
  • Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler: Places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs): Provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions.

The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA. Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies; prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers.

⚙️ Key details

  • Deployment Paths: Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints. Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment.
  • Inference Engines: You can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts.
  • Configuration: Both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. Dynamo-specific settings belong under spec.dynamoSpec. For example, a configuration might run one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs) with two frontend replicas for request handling. Setting dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode to kv-aware turns on KV-aware routing.
  • Health Management: HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers.

💡 Why it matters

For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product. “For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.” — Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability

Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block that you can use on its own or chain together.

  • Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score.
  • Human Review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports.
  • Synthetic Data Generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale.
  • Data Quality Evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage.
  • Data Transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale.

#SageMaker #NVIDIA #Dynamo #Inference #DataPreparation

item.title: Databricks Solution Accelerator Enables Real-Time Next-Best-Offer Recommenders
item.description:
Databricks Solution Accelerator Enables Real-Time Next-Best-Offer Recommenders

Databricks has released an open-source Solution Accelerator that uses Feature Views to build a real-time next-best-offer (NBO) recommender for financial services. The solution addresses the challenge of real-time personalization by allowing developers to define features once for both training and serving, preventing duplicate definitions that can drift over time.

🔍 Overview

The accelerator enables a system that ranks a catalog of offers—including credit card upgrades, savings products, and personal loans—based on in-session intent. When a retail banking customer checks their accounts, explores credit cards, or opens a loan calculator, these interactions signal current intent. The system ensures that relevant offers reach the customer while they are still in the session. The accelerator includes two main parts: a recommender using batch features and an extension that adds streaming, in-session intent. Both are built end-to-end on Databricks with runnable notebooks that users can clone and deploy.

🧩 How it Works

Raw clickstream data is aggregated into time-windowed features for two purposes: training on historical values as they existed at a given point in time, and serving predictions using current values with millisecond latency. To avoid train/serve skew, which can degrade model accuracy, features must be computed the same way during training and serving. Databricks Feature Views eliminate the need for separate feature definitions by letting users define features once for both contexts.

The training process uses the create_training_set API, which retrieves feature values as they existed at each labeled event to prevent future data leakage. This utilizes the Feature Engineering SDK to reconstruct feature values via a point-in-time join. The resulting training set feeds a LightGBM ranker registered in Unity Catalog. At inference time, the Model Serving endpoint fetches batch features from the online store using customer_id and scores all 40 offers directly without an additional candidate-narrowing step. Each request contains the customer_id, candidate offers, and session context.

⚙️ Key Details

The architecture supports specific performance and structural requirements:

  • Latency: One declarative definition powers point-in-time training and warm online ranking at p95 34 ms, with in-session signals live in under 130 ms.
  • Model: A single ranking model combines stable customer context (balances, spending, tenure, and risk band) with recent clickstream activity.
  • Optimization: SawtoothWindow keeps longer streaming windows practical, allowing a 30-day category count to stay fresh as new events arrive without recomputing entire history.
  • Structure: The accelerator consists of three steps delivered as runnable notebooks across two parts that share a catalog, schema, online store, and feature definitions.

💡 Why it Matters

Real-time personalization depends on understanding what customers want in the moment. By ensuring that features are computed identically for offline training and online serving, organizations can maintain model accuracy while serving predictions with millisecond latency. The shared definitions reduce the risk of feature drift that typically occurs when training and serving pipelines are built separately.

item.title: SAP and Infosys Argue Enterprise AI Needs Unified Data and Governance
item.description:
SAP and Infosys Argue Enterprise AI Needs Unified Data and Governance

SAP and Infosys executives are advocating for a shift in how enterprises approach AI, moving away from isolated pilots toward a unified platform model that integrates data, governance, and business processes.

🧩 From Pilots to Enterprise Platform

For years, organizations have treated AI as a series of discrete experiments. However, as AI agents begin to move into workflows that run the business, that model is becoming inadequate. The core challenge now is rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together to turn AI into part of the enterprise operating model.

Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, notes that many customers struggle to convert interest in AI into an operationalized model because programs often start as isolated proof-of-concepts (POCs) on inconsistent and fragmented data foundations. This fragmentation leads to duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale.

⚙️ Key Components of the Shift

  • Unified Data Layer: Leiduck argues that AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. Companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes.
  • Governance and Oversight: Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. Leiduck and Singh agree that the absence of governance does not speed up adoption but instead creates a “risk backlog” that can force disruptive stops and audits.
  • Evaluation Framework: Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, recommends evaluating AI use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies must identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, ensure their data and talent can support the use case, and establish whether successful applications can be replicated.

💡 Why It Matters

As AI moves into mission-critical workflows, the stakes change significantly. Leiduck points out that while “80% might be good enough” for everyday applications, that level of accuracy is a “very terrible result” in areas such as supply chains or financial close. The goal is to move beyond AI as a mere productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner” that helps leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. Customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data are becoming critical enterprise assets in this future.

#EnterpriseAI #AIAgents #SAP #Infosys #DataGovernance

Source: Building AI that can work across the enterprise

item.title: SDGym Benchmarking Framework Released for Synthetic Data Evaluation
item.description:
SDGym Benchmarking Framework Released for Synthetic Data Evaluation

The Synthetic Data Vault Project from DataCebo has introduced SDGym (Synthetic Data Gym), a benchmarking framework designed to model and generate synthetic data. This tool allows developers to measure performance, memory usage, and data quality across various modeling techniques, including classical statistics and deep learning.

🔍 Overview

SDGym integrates with the Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) ecosystem, providing a way to evaluate synthesizers, datasets, and metrics. The project traces its origins to MIT’s Data to AI Lab in 2016, with DataCebo founded in 2020 to grow the ecosystem, which is now described as the largest for synthetic data generation and evaluation.

🧩 How it works

The framework allows users to benchmark techniques by selecting synthesizers and baselines, then running evaluations on publicly available or custom datasets. Key workflow steps include:

  • Defining which modeling techniques to use, such as GaussianCopulaSynthesizer and CTGANSynthesizer.
  • Selecting baselines, such as UniformSynthesizer.
  • Executing the benchmark using the function sdgym.benchmark_single_table.
  • Generating a detailed evaluation of performance, memory, and quality across the selected datasets.

Users can also customize the process by writing their own machine learning models, specifying training and sampling logic to test personal synthetic data generation techniques.

⚙️ Key details

  • Metrics: Measures performance, memory usage, synthetic data quality, and privacy.
  • Data Sources: Supports publicly available datasets from the SDV project and custom private datasets stored locally or on Amazon S3.
  • Customization: Allows users to include their own synthesizers, datasets, or metrics.
  • Installation: Available via pip or conda, with a recommendation to use a virtual environment to avoid software conflicts.

🚀 Availability

SDGym is part of the SDV library ecosystem. Developers can access the documentation and install the package to begin benchmarking immediately. The library includes a feature to list available datasets, facilitating quick setup for users wishing to test against standard public data.

item.title: Serverless Model Context Protocol Server Enables Shared Enterprise Data Access for AI Agents
item.description:
Serverless Model Context Protocol Server Enables Shared Enterprise Data Access for AI Agents

Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application.

🔍 Overview

  • “Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between.”
  • Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control.
  • As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi‑day engineering effort.
  • Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow.
  • To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate.

🧩 How it works

  1. Client layer – users submit a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53, reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet (HTTPS + AWS WAF), then routes to Amazon Cognito for authentication and enrichment. Authenticated traffic enters a private subnet where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate, stores session state in Amazon DynamoDB, and forwards requests through an internal ALB to the MCP server layer.
  2. MCP server layer – an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction.
  3. Tools layer – Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift execute SQL against the data lake; Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (RAG) handles semantic search. AWS Lambda ingests data into Amazon S3 and the knowledge bases.
  4. Knowledge‑base refresh layer – a metadata catalog stores schema descriptions, column‑level semantics, and table relationships. It is refreshed continuously, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives.
  5. When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to those tables, reducing noise and improving SQL generation accuracy.

⚙️ Key details

  • “Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code.”
  • Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer, providing a single audit point.
  • The metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, allowing the agent to derive schema knowledge at query time – no hard‑coded table structures or redeployment when schemas change.
  • The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge‑base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable.
  • In testing, this scoping keeps end‑to‑end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range.
  • The data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain‑specific data.

🚀 Availability & Deployment

  • The MCP server is deployed serverlessly on Amazon ECS Fargate, eliminating the need for provisioned servers.
  • Public‑to‑private subnet routing ensures secure handling of authenticated traffic.
  • Amazon Route 53, Application Load Balancers, AWS WAF, Amazon Cognito, DynamoDB, Athena, Redshift, Bedrock Guardrails, and Lambda are all managed services that contribute to a fully managed solution.
  • FastMCP provides the framework for building MCP servers in Python, and Amazon Bedrock supplies the underlying LLM capabilities.

This implementation removes duplicated integration code, centralizes access control, and shortens onboarding of new datasets from multi‑day efforts to a simple metadata file drop.

#AIAgents #ModelContextProtocol #AWS #EnterpriseData

Source: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Property Finder uncovers label bias and improves vision AI with Amazon Bedrock
item.description:
Property Finder uncovers label bias and improves vision AI with Amazon Bedrock

Property Finder’s engineering team discovered that 96.8 percent of their image‑evaluation labels were inherited directly from a single vision‑language model instead of being verified by human experts. By building an unbiased ground‑truth set and applying evolutionary prompt optimization on Amazon Bedrock, they achieved higher accuracy while cutting costs by 86 percent.

🔍 Overview

  • Co‑authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder.
  • The issue was uncovered while migrating the vision AI workload to a more cost‑effective option on Amazon Bedrock.
  • Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images each day across the MENA region, with thousands of new listings averaging 15 images that must be quality‑checked before going live.

🏗️ Evaluation Bias Discovery

  • 96.8 % of the existing evaluation labels came from the predictions of a single VLM, never independently verified.
  • This left any alternative model structurally disadvantaged before any image was processed.
  • Specific problems identified:
    • Watermark text extraction showed character‑level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters.
    • Photo classification forced a single label onto images that contained multiple room types.
    • In the remaining 3.2 % of human‑labeled samples, annotators introduced categories outside the original specification (e.g., “Office” where no such label existed in the prompt).

🛠️ Building Unbiased Ground Truth

  • The team hand‑annotated 356 UAE images and a separate set of Egypt images, selected from unlabeled production listings across representative industry segments.
  • The first 256 UAE images formed the development set for prompt tuning.
  • An evaluation set uses all 356 images plus 100 newly annotated images to compare the final model.
  • A strategy and analytics expert annotated all images; the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team performed systematic quality reviews to resolve ambiguous cases and keep labeling consistent.
  • A set of 356 images is considered roughly sufficient to detect moderate differences between models.

🤖 Prompt Optimization on Amazon Bedrock

  • Property Finder processed each image with Amazon Bedrock, which returns predicted attributes in JSON format.
  • During optimization, predictions were scored with Micro F1 against the 256‑image expert‑annotated development set.
  • The optimization loop ran from v0 to v27:
    • Early versions used AI assistants to refine prompts.
    • Later versions employed automated optimization.
  • Switching from single‑label to multi‑label classification removed a major source of artificial ambiguity and allowed measurement of correct secondary predictions.

📊 Results

  • The selected model on Amazon Bedrock delivered higher accuracy while reducing inference cost by 86 percent compared with the legacy approach.
  • The unbiased ground‑truth data eliminated the structural disadvantage previously faced by alternative models.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Property Finder evaluates 11 quality attributes per image, covering:
    • Watermark detection
    • Room classification
    • Furnishing status
    • Photo quality
    • Construction indicators
  • Reliable quality assessment is essential for tens of thousands of daily listings before they appear to users.
  • A hybrid approach—combining models from different families, surfacing candidate labels and disagreements, and having human experts adjudicate—ensures no model output is used directly as a label.

Attribute Coverage (sample)

Attribute Category Example
Watermark detection Detects embedded branding or text watermarks
Room classification Identifies living room, kitchen, bedroom, etc.
Furnishing status Determines whether a room is furnished
Photo quality Assesses resolution, lighting, and composition
Construction indicators Flags signs of construction or renovation

#PropertyFinder #ComputerVision #AmazonBedrock #DataQuality

Source: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA KvikIO Python Library Demonstrates Direct GPU Storage Access via GPUDirect Storage
item.description:
NVIDIA KvikIO Python Library Demonstrates Direct GPU Storage Access via GPUDirect Storage

NVIDIA’s Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) now works with the KvikIO Python library to let AI applications move data directly from storage into GPU memory, bypassing the CPU.

🔍 Overview

  • GPU applications are processing ever‑growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators.
  • The 2025 Stanford AI Index reports that compute for notable AI models has been doubling roughly every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling roughly every eight months.
  • As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
  • NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory.
  • The direct path avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system.
  • GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many major storage vendors.
  • At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development; as of August 2025, nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python.

🧩 How It Works

Component Role
GPUDirect Storage (GDS) Enables a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory.
cuFile C library and API through which applications and frameworks access GDS.
KvikIO Python and C++ library that sits above cuFile, providing high‑level, idiomatic interfaces and additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.
  • The application supplies a file‑system path and a GPU buffer.
  • KvikIO decides whether to route the request through cuFile (direct path) or use its POSIX compatibility path, which stages data through host memory.
  • When cuFile is selected, KvikIO registers the file and issues the I/O using the target GPU buffer.
  • cuFile then determines the actual transfer path based on system support, the file system, and its configuration; it may use the accelerated GDS path or fall back to a CPU‑staged compatibility path.
  • Reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.

⚙️ Tutorial Highlights

  • Demonstrates how to use the NVIDIA KvikIO Python API to configure storage I/O, read data into GPU memory, and confirm that the accelerated path within GDS was activated.
  • Shows how to inspect KvikIO and cuFile settings that influence the path each operation takes.
  • Tested on an x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18.
  • The system used a local NVMe device formatted with ext4; a PIX connection between the GPU and NVMe device means the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge.
  • IOMMU and ACS were disabled to preserve PCIe peer‑to‑peer transfers, and the nvidia-fs kernel module was loaded to provide the accelerated path.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Doubling compute and dataset sizes increase pressure on the storage‑to‑GPU data pipeline.
  • Direct storage‑to‑GPU transfers reduce CPU overhead, freeing CPU resources for other parts of the AI workload.
  • Providing a high‑level Python interface (KvikIO) aligns with the fact that nearly half of new AI projects are Python‑centric, lowering the barrier for developers to adopt accelerated I/O.
  • A growing storage‑vendor ecosystem around GDS broadens hardware compatibility for future AI systems.

#NVIDIA #GPUDirectStorage #KvikIO #AI #Python

Source: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Foundation Model Beats Traditional Pipelines on Enterprise Databases
item.description:
NVIDIA Kumo Relational Foundation Model Beats Traditional Pipelines on Enterprise Databases

NVIDIA introduced Kumo Relational, a pre‑trained relational foundation model that predicts directly on enterprise databases without task‑specific training or feature engineering.

🔍 Overview

  • Operates on the database itself, respecting tables, foreign keys, and timestamps.
  • Accepts a Predictive Query Language (PQL) statement that describes what to predict rather than how.
  • Returns predictions in a single forward pass after gathering up to 10,000 historical examples as context.

🧩 How it Works

  • Pre‑training: Trained once on synthetic relational data that mirrors real‑world datasets.
  • In‑context learning: At inference time the model reads up to 10,000 context examples, each consisting of a local subgraph around an entity and its ground‑truth target (e.g., churn, demand, fraud).
  • Temporal handling: For time‑based tasks the model replays historical database states, sampling entity‑centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and using only data from before that point to avoid leakage.
  • Architecture: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction.
  • Agent integration: Built to be called by agents; the PQL interface provides a simple way for agents to ask predictive questions.

⚙️ Performance

Benchmark Metric Improvement over baseline
RelBench V1 classification AUROC +~4 points vs. gradient‑boosted trees on expert‑engineered features
SAP SALT (out‑of‑the‑box) MRR +7 points vs. XGBoost on engineered features
SAP SALT (fine‑tuned) MRR +13 points vs. XGBoost
41 tasks on 15 databases (overall) MRR +8% vs. AutoGluon ensembles

Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, Kumo Relational beats supervised relational deep‑learning models, expert‑engineered gradient‑boosted tree pipelines, and AutoGluon ensembles. It also outperforms gradient‑boosted trees on RelBench V1 by nearly 4 AUROC points on average.

🚀 Availability

  • Accessible through NVIDIA’s open‑source, GPU‑native structured‑data‑models library.
  • Also offered as an NVIDIA NIM (NVIDIA Inference Model).
  • Scales to databases with 500 B+ rows and works for both humans and agents.
  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

💡 Why it Matters

  • Eliminates weeks of feature engineering, task‑specific training, and pipeline tuning traditionally required for relational data.
  • A single pre‑trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks, turning a new prediction into a query rather than a full project.
  • Demonstrates that foundation models for structured data can outperform the best supervised models, simplifying production deployment and enabling broader use of predictive analytics across organizations.

#NVIDIA #RelationalAI #MachineLearning #EnterpriseAI

Source: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required

item.title: NVIDIA and IIT Madras Release 2.8 Trillion‑Token Indic Pretraining Corpus

NVIDIA and IIT Madras Release 2.8 Trillion‑Token Indic Pretraining Corpus

NVIDIA, in collaboration with IIT Madras and its AI4Bharat lab, is releasing Nemotron‑pretraining‑Indic‑v1, a 2.8 trillion‑token dataset covering all 22 Indian Constitution languages, together with an open GPU‑accelerated data‑generation pipeline.

🔍 Overview

  • Approx. 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages (the languages listed in India’s Constitution, spoken by 97 % of Indians – about 1.2 billion citizens at the 2011 Census).\
  • Developed by NVIDIA, IIT Madras, and AI4Bharat.\
  • Released alongside an open, GPU‑accelerated synthetic‑data pipeline that captures prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks.\
  • Extends prior resources such as AI4Bharat’s Sangraha open pretraining corpus.

🧩 How it works

  • The pipeline is built with NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA’s open‑source framework for generating synthetic data.\
  • It follows a four‑stage synthetic‑data workflow (translation → quality assessment → targeted repair → final validation) implemented using Gemma‑4‑31B‑it.\
  • Each output retains a source identifier, allowing developers to trace synthetic text back to its original document.\
  • Quality checks preserve technical content such as equations, tables, and code.

⚙️ Key details

  • Token composition (Gemma‑4 tokenizer):\
    • 2,601.0 billion native‑script tokens\

item.title: Guide to Building Production AI Memory Systems
item.description:
Guide to Building Production AI Memory Systems

AI language models are stateless, so every request starts from a blank slate. What feels like memory in a chat window is actually an application trick that resends earlier messages. To give assistants persistent, user‑specific knowledge, developers add a separate engineering layer called an AI memory system. This guide explains the components, workflow, and practical considerations for deploying such a system in production.

🔍 Overview

  • Definition – An AI memory system is a storage and retrieval layer that lets an AI application save useful information, retrieve the relevant parts later, and use them to improve future responses.
  • Stateless models – Large language models are stateless by design; every request receives a prompt, produces a completion, and retains nothing. This is true of GPT‑style models, Claude, Gemini, and open‑source models such as Llama and Mistral alike.
  • Illusion of chat memory – What looks like memory in a chat window is an illusion produced by the application, which resends the earlier messages with each new request. That approach hits a hard ceiling because context windows are finite, long prompts cost more and respond slower, and models tend to use information in the middle of a very long context less reliably than information at the edges.

🧩 How it works

The core of every memory system follows a six‑step pipeline:

Step Description
Capture After each interaction, an extractor decides whether anything is worth keeping and rewrites it as a clean, self‑contained statement (e.g., “Prefers deployment on AWS.”).
Store The statement and its metadata (user ID, timestamp, source, confidence) are stored in a vector database.
Index An embedding model converts the text into a vector, placing similar meanings close together.
Retrieve At query time the system looks for the closest matches, then re‑ranks them by relevance, recency, and importance.
Inject The top memories are formatted into the prompt within a strict token budget.
Generate The language model generates a response using the injected memories; the memory lives in the prompt for minutes and is limited by the context window.

⚙️ Key details

  • External decision making – The memory system decides what to save, where to keep it, and what to place in front of the model on each turn.
  • Memory types –
    • Episodic memory lets an agent learn from experience rather than start over each time.
    • Distilled facts and domain knowledge such as “the user writes Python” or “refunds are allowed within 30 days.”
  • Memory updates – New facts are compared with old ones; duplicates are merged, contradictions are resolved, and stale items are expired.
  • Production definition – A governed data service with write policies, retrieval quality metrics, expiration rules, access controls, and user‑facing edit and delete tools.

💡 Why it matters

  • Without a memory system, developers must rely on ever‑growing prompts, which incur higher costs, slower responses, and reduced reliability of information deep inside the context.
  • An external memory can persist for months or years, enabling assistants to adapt to individual users over long periods.
  • Adding a memory layer transforms a stateless language model into an assistant that remembers preferences, policies, and domain facts across sessions.

#AImemory #LLM #ProductionAI

Source: AI Memory Systems: The Practical Guide to Architecture and Real-World Examples - Dealon.ai

item.title: NVIDIA KGMON Team Secures Second Place at KDD Cup 2026 with Agent Harness
item.description:
NVIDIA KGMON Team Secures Second Place at KDD Cup 2026 with Agent Harness

The NVIDIA KGMON team placed second in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents competition with a system that streamlines the agent harness to be smaller, clearer, and easier to verify.

🔍 Overview

  • The competition required agents to answer natural‑language questions over heterogeneous data sources such as databases, CSV/JSON files, prose documents, PDFs, and briefing videos.
  • Every task demanded more than simple retrieval: agents had to inspect data, choose appropriate tools, reason across sources, produce a final answer file, and navigate traps common in analytical workflows.
  • Teams were limited to a small, fixed LLM, making the harness the primary optimization surface.
  • KGMON’s approach focused on preprocessing, constrained tools, persistent state, and systematic evaluation to make the task easier for the available model.

🛠️ Architecture & Workflow

  • Unified data access – CSV and JSON files were converted into tables inside a single SQLite database, giving the agent one SQL interface for all structured data.
  • Single tool set – The environment exposed only a few helpers: schema inspection, SQL queries, document lookup, prose extraction, and answer writing.
  • Schema‑scouting step – Before the main reasoning loop the system inspected tables, columns, join keys, duplicate names, units, null patterns, and row‑grain issues, then supplied this context to the agent.
  • Middleware repair – Malformed tool calls were automatically fixed so a single bad call would not abort the attempt.
  • Stateful Python environment – Variables persisted between tool calls, allowing reuse of intermediate results.
  • Predefined functions – schema(), sql(query), and write_answer(df) reduced boilerplate, syntax errors, and file‑handling mistakes.
  • Execution tracing – Repeated attempts and trajectory inspection helped identify failures and refine the harness.
Function / Helper Role
schema() Provide the agent with table and column metadata discovered during scouting
sql(query) Execute a SQL statement against the unified SQLite database
write_answer(df) Write the final answer file in the required format
Document lookup Retrieve relevant prose or PDF content
Prose extraction Pull specific text snippets from unstructured documents

Figure 1 (see below) illustrates the overall workflow from data ingestion to final answer generation.

⚙️ Reliability Techniques

  • Preprocessing data into a uniform SQL schema reduced routing failures and saved turns for reasoning.
  • Constrained tool set limited the ways the agent could interact with the environment, lowering the chance of mistakes.
  • Persistent state and middleware repair prevented a single error from ending an attempt.
  • Short, valid attempts conserved the limited turn budget for additional runs, evaluation, and ensembling.
  • Execution traces and trajectory inspection were used to pinpoint failures such as bad tool calls or answer‑format issues.

🚩 Common Failure Modes

  • Bad tool call (e.g., syntax error)
  • Incorrect join key leading to wrong results
  • Missed document rule or threshold in unstructured sources
  • Answer‑format mismatch causing the final output to be rejected

💡 Why It Matters

  • The techniques are especially useful when building reliable systems around smaller open models.
  • Reliability often stems more from a well‑designed harness than from expanding the openness of the model itself.
  • A streamlined harness leaves more capacity for the fixed LLM to focus on analysis rather than plumbing.

item.title: QAD ERP Reporting Extends to Microsoft Fabric via Open Mirroring
item.description:
QAD ERP Reporting Extends to Microsoft Fabric via Open Mirroring

Manufacturers using QAD ERP can combine multiple reporting layers, and a new mirroring path now moves QAD data into Microsoft Fabric.

🔍 Overview

  • Layer 1 – Native QAD tools – Provide operational lookups, formatted documents and financial statements inside the ERP.
  • Layer 2 – Power BI – Adds interactive analysis; the simplest connection imports QAD data over OpenEdge ODBC on a schedule.
  • Layer 3 – Data warehouse / Microsoft Fabric – Uses a QAD Fabric mirroring process that runs through Open Mirroring because Microsoft Fabric has no native mirroring source for QAD.

🧩 How it works

  1. An extraction layer reads tables from the Progress OpenEdge database behind QAD.
  2. It writes those tables as Parquet files into a landing zone in OneLake.
  3. Microsoft Fabric turns the Parquet files into Delta tables and keeps them current.
  4. Each table requires a stable key.

⚙️ Key details

  • The three layers can be used simultaneously by a manufacturer.
  • Power BI connects via OpenEdge ODBC and can be scheduled for regular imports.
  • Fabric mirroring relies on Open Mirroring; there is no built‑in source connector for QAD.
  • Delta tables in Fabric provide a continuously refreshed view of the ERP data.

📊 Layer comparison

Layer What it provides Integration method
Native QAD tools Operational lookups, formatted documents, financial statements Built‑in ERP functionality
Power BI Interactive analysis OpenEdge ODBC import on a schedule
Microsoft Fabric Mirrored, current Delta tables Open Mirroring → Parquet → OneLake → Delta

💡 Why it matters

  • Combining native ERP reports with Power BI and Fabric gives manufacturers flexible, up‑to‑date analytics.
  • The mirroring flow keeps the data warehouse synchronized without a native QAD connector.
  • Stable keys ensure reliable table joins and updates within Fabric.

#QAD #MicrosoftFabric #PowerBI #DataMirroring

item.title: End-to-End Approach for Generating Context-Specific LLM Benchmark Datasets
item.description:
End-to-End Approach for Generating Context-Specific LLM Benchmark Datasets

A new paper presents an end-to-end approach for creating large language model (LLM) benchmark datasets by combining synthetic data generation with expert input.

💡 Why it matters

Existing benchmark construction methods typically face a trade-off between validity and scalability:

  • Expert-designed datasets: Produce high-quality evaluations but are slow and costly to create.
  • Synthetically generated data: Scale efficiently but often result in redundant, unrealistic, or out-of-scope examples.

🧩 How it works

To address these gaps, the approach utilizes the following mechanisms:

  • Schema Elicitation: A schema is used to elicit key information regarding the context, scope, and goals of an evaluation task, which then guides the synthetic data generation.
